threads.body: Including `stability` in the `warnOnce` key means the same deprecated property can emit two separate warnings (one per stability) within the same JVM, which can reintroduce log noise even though the deprecated setting itself is always experimental. If the goal is \"warn once per deprecated property\", consider removing `stability` from the dedupe key (keep it just `flatProperty + \":deprecated\"`) and, if necessary, adjust the message to be correct for both modes (e.g., mention the stable replacement while still pointing out the experimental deprecated key).

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: The current head already uses `flatProperty + ":deprecated"` as the warning key. Stability affects only the replacement property in the message, so the deprecated property emits at most one warning per JVM.

Upsides: This keeps warning deduplication tied to the deprecated property while preserving the correct stable or experimental replacement in the first warning.

Downsides: No material downside identified.

Consider using the project’s existing test isolation mechanism (e.g., a JUnit resource lock / non-parallel annotation for this test/class) or a scoped system-properties helper so the mutation is serialized.

threads.body: The `warnOnce` key (`flatProperty + ":deprecated"`) does not incorporate the *selected replacement* (`replacementFlatProperties` / stability). If the same deprecated capture property is encountered in both STABLE and EXPERIMENTAL contexts within the same JVM, only the first message will be logged and may point users to the wrong replacement property names. Consider including stability (or the replacement property string) in the dedupe key (e.g., `flatProperty + ":deprecated:" + stability`) so the warning consistently references the correct replacement for the caller.

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: The deprecated flat property identifies one instrumentation and selector. That instrumentation chooses one replacement stability when it calls `resolve`, so the first warning points to the replacement for the caller that applied the deprecated value. Keying by the replacement would emit duplicate warnings for the same deprecated setting if inconsistent callers used both modes.

Upsides: Warning volume remains bounded to one message per deprecated property while the message still names the replacement selected by the applying caller.

Downsides: If one instrumentation incorrectly resolves the same selector in both stability modes, only the first caller's migration path is logged.

Consider including stability (or `replacementFlatProperties`) in the `warnOnce` key so STABLE and EXPERIMENTAL warnings don’t dedupe each other incorrectly.

threads.body: The expected warning message mixes stable and experimental property prefixes: the included property is missing the `.experimental.` segment while the excluded property includes it. `SelectorConfig.resolveLegacyBoolean(...)` passes `Stability.EXPERIMENTAL` into the replacement properties, so both included and excluded should use the experimental prefix (or neither should if the production output changed accordingly). Update the assertion string to match the actual replacement properties emitted by `selectorFlatProperties(..., Stability.EXPERIMENTAL)`.

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: The included prefix is split between adjacent string literals: `otel.instrumentation.boolean-enabled.experimental` plus `.key-value-pair-attributes.included` yields the full experimental property. The excluded prefix uses `otel.instrumentation.boolean-enabled` plus `.experimental.key-value-pair-attributes.excluded`, which yields the same experimental prefix. The production helper constructs both with `Stability.EXPERIMENTAL`, and the focused test passed on the current head.

Upsides: This avoids changing an assertion that already exactly matches the emitted warning.

Downsides: Different line-break placement makes the two equivalent prefixes less obvious in the source.
